103.t: From Proto-Hellenic *dúwo, from Proto-Indo-European *duwó, a variant of *dwóh₁. Cognates include Sanskrit द्व (dvá), Old Armenian երկու (erku), Latin duo, and Old English twā (English two).

137.t: According to Beekes, a Pre-Greek substrate borrowing tentatively reconstructed as *talakʸa; the element "-σσ-", as well as the local geographic meaning, points to a Pre-Greek origin.

107.t: Originally the neuter accusative plural of ἄλλος (állos, “another, different”) with shifted accent in an adverbial sense, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂élyos (“other”).

176.t: Univerbation of δι’ (di’), apocopic form of διά (diá, “because of”), and ὅτι (hóti, “that”, conjunction).

126.t: From Proto-Hellenic *pā́wits. Cognates include Latin puer, Sanskrit पु॒त्र (putrá, “son”), and Avestan 𐬞𐬎𐬚𐬭𐬀 (puθra, “son”).

167.t: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *pnew- Proto-Indo-European *-mn̥ Proto-Indo-European *pnéwmn̥ Proto-Hellenic *pnéumə Ancient Greek πνεῦμα From Proto-Hellenic *pnéumə, from Proto-Indo-European *pnéwmn̥, from *pnew-.

169.t: From the root of θνῄσκω (thnēískō, “to die”), with the suffix from Proto-Indo-European *-etos, also seen in βίοτος (bíotos, “life”).

188.t: From Proto-Hellenic *mā́tēr (compare Mycenaean Greek 𐀔𐀳𐀩 (ma-te-re), Doric μάτηρ (mā́tēr)), from Proto-Indo-European *méh₂tēr.

175.t: From προ- (pro-, “before”) + φημί (phēmí, “to say”) + -της (-tēs, “-er”, masculine agent-noun suffix).

144.t: From Proto-Hellenic *kʰepʰəlā́, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰebʰ-l̥ (“head”) + *-éh₂ (“nominal suffix”). Compare κεβλή (keblḗ).

199.t: Probably formed innovatively from πλήθω (plḗthō, “to fill”) + -ος (-os). Compare the relationship between πλῆθος (plêthos) ~ πλήθω (plḗthō) ~ πέπληθα (péplētha) and βριθύς (brithús, “heavy”) ~ βρίθω (bríthō) ~ βέβριθα (bébritha).

134.t: By surface analysis, φόβος (phóbos) + -έω (-éō). From Proto-Hellenic *pʰogʷéyō, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰogʷéyeti, from *bʰegʷ-.

173.t: From Proto-Hellenic *tréyes, from Proto-Indo-European *tréyes. Cognates include Sanskrit त्रि (tri), Latin trēs, Old Armenian երեք (erekʻ) and Old English þrēo (English three).

179.t: From Proto-Hellenic *heptə́, from Proto-Indo-European *septḿ̥. Cognates include Latin septem, Sanskrit सप्त (saptá), Old Armenian եաւթն (eawtʻn), Old English seofon (English seven).

186.t: From Proto-Hellenic *grə́pʰō, from Proto-Indo-European *gerbʰ-. Cognates include Old English ċeorfan (English carve), Old Church Slavonic жрѣбъ (žrěbŭ).

113.t: Possibly from Proto-Hellenic *əgatʰós, from Proto-Indo-European *m̥ǵh₂dʰh₁ós (“made great; whose deeds are great”), from *méǵh₂s (“great”) + *dʰeh₁- (“do”) + *-ós. Compare Latin magnificus from same roots.

104.t: From Proto-Hellenic *wérgon, from Proto-Indo-European *wérǵom. Cognates include Old English weorc (English work), Avestan 𐬬𐬀𐬭𐬆𐬰𐬆𐬨 (var^əzəm) (Persian وَرز (varz)), and Old Armenian գործ (gorc).

146.t: Borrowed from Biblical Hebrew יַעֲקֹב (yaʿăqōḇ). While Ἰακώβ (Iakṓb) refers to Jacob and Ἰάκωβος (Iákōbos) to James in the Greek writings, both English names derive from Ἰάκωβος (Iákōbos), which is derived from Ἰακώβ (Iakṓb).

161.t: The origin is unknown, with multiple theories proposed: * From a Proto-Indo-European *kaḱ-, *knḱ- (“slight”), and related to Avestan 𐬐𐬀𐬯𐬎 (kasu, “small, slight”). * From Proto-Indo-European *kenk- (“to burn, hunger, desire”), and related to Lithuanian…

106.t: Inchoative present (with suffix -σκω (-skō)) formed from the aorist εὗρον (heûron). The exact formation of the word's root is unclear, appearing to be a reduplicative of a Proto-Indo-European *wreh₁- (“to find”).

195.t: Unknown. Has been compared to λεῖος (leîos, “smooth”), λιτός (lītós, “simple; plain”), Latin laedō (“to strike; to hurt”), Lithuanian slidùs (“slippery; slick”), Proto-Balto-Slavic *ledús (“ice”).

148.t: Uncertain and contested, as many competing theories exist.

139.t: From Proto-Hellenic *hupér, from Proto-Indo-European *upér (“over, above”), from *upo (“under, below”) (whence English up). Cognates include Latin super and Proto-Germanic *uber (whence English over).

100.t: From earlier *αἰϝών (*aiwṓn), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eyu- (“vital force, life, long life, eternity”), whence also ἀεί (aeí, “always”). Cognate with Latin aevum, English aye.

118.t: From Proto-Hellenic *pāwər, from Proto-Indo-European *péh₂wr̥. The noun was changed to a pure R-stem noun; if it retained the oblique N-stem forms of its ancestor, its oblique base would have been **πυν- (**pŭn-).

122.t: From Proto-Indo-European *upó (“under, below”), with regular rough breathing ῾ (h) before initial υ (u). Cognates include Latin sub and Sanskrit उप (úpa).

153.t: Some suggest that this form comes from the original imperative *ἔσθι (*ésthi) of ἔδω (édō), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ed- (“to eat”).

154.t: From Proto-Hellenic *píptō, from Proto-Indo-European *pípth₂-, reduplicated present from *peth₂- (“to fall; to fly”). For an unknown reason, the iota is long, as is apparent from the imperative πῖπτε (not **πίπτε (**pĭ́pte)).

147.t: From εὐ- (eu-, “good, well”) + λόγος (lógos, “speech”) + -έω (-éō, denominative verbal suffix). Compare εὔλογος (eúlogos, “reasonable, sensible”).

112.t: From Proto-Hellenic *métsos, from Proto-Indo-European *médʰyos (“between”). Cognate with Latin medius, Sanskrit मध्य (madhya), Avestan 𐬨𐬀𐬌𐬜𐬌𐬌𐬁𐬥𐬀 (maⁱδiiāna), Old Armenian մէջ (mēǰ), etc.

136.t: Related to Mycenaean Greek 𐀈𐀁𐀫 (do-e-ro /⁠dohelos⁠/), possibly from Canaanite *dōʾēlu “servant, attendant” (compare Late Babylonian 𒁕𒀝𒂵𒇻 (daggālu, “subject, one who waits on another, does their bidding”).

141.t: Perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *dóḱs(e)h₂, from *deḱ- (“to accept”) (whence δοκέω (dokéō)) or with some other influence directly from δοκέω (dokéō).

101.t: The stem ἵ- (hí-) is probably from Proto-Indo-European *Hyós (“that, who, which”), while the ending is an instrumental ending found in Sanskrit येन॑ (yéna, “by which; by that”), Old High German hina (“thither”), Old Irish cen (“on this side”).

142.t: From Proto-Indo-European *bʰuH-lom, from *bʰuH- (“to be, grow”). By surface analysis, an old derivative from φῦναι (phûnai), active infinitive of an aorist form ἔφυν (éphūn) of φύω (phŭ́ō, “to bring forth”).

163.t: According to Beekes, of Pre-Greek origin, as suggested by πτ ~ π (pt ~ p) variation in its variants.

157.t: From the stem of βασιλεύς (basileús, “king”) + -ία (-íā, abstract noun suffix).

193.t: From Proto-Hellenic *dḗ, from Proto-Indo-European *de (“instrumental particle”). See also δέ (dé).

162.t: Of uncertain origin. Based on the architectural semantic domain of the term, probably a Pre-Greek loan.

124.t: From Proto-Hellenic *hékʰō, from Proto-Indo-European *séǵʰeti, from Proto-Indo-European *seǵʰ-. Compare Mycenaean Greek 𐀃𐀏 (o-ka) and 𐀁𐀐𐀁 (e-ke-e).

168.t: From διατίθημι (dĭătĭ́thēmĭ); also analyzable as δια- (dia-) + -θήκη (-thḗkē)

131.t: Usually said to be a derivative of Proto-Indo-European *(s)ḱeh₃- (“shade, shadow”), originally referring to a light construction of cloth hung between tree branches to provide a shadow which could be used for shelter and other activities, though the…

109.t: From Proto-Hellenic *títʰēmi, *tétʰēmi, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰé-dʰeh₁-ti, reduplicated present from *dʰeh₁- (“to put, place”). The pay/offer senses are from conflation with δίδωμι (dídōmi) in PIE, see Latin -dō.

111.t: Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *wer- (“to watch, guard”). There may have been an intermediate form *ϝοράω (*worắō), from Proto-Hellenic *worā́ō.

192.t: From Proto-Hellenic *téknon, from Proto-Indo-European *teḱ-, perhaps via τίκτω (tíktō, “I bear”). Cognates include Old English þegn (“servant”), Old High German degan and possibly Sanskrit तोक (toka, “offspring, child”).

177.t: From Proto-Hellenic *tʰūmós, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰuh₂mós (“smoke”). Cognates include Sanskrit धूम (dhūmá), Lithuanian dūmas, Latin fūmus, Old Church Slavonic дꙑмъ (dymŭ) and Albanian tym.

158.t: From Proto-Indo-European *h₂énti (“front, opposite”). Cognates include English and, Latin ante, Sanskrit अन्ति (ánti), and Old Armenian ընդ (ənd).

190.t: Uncertain. Could be from unattested *ζατός (*zātós), from the same root of δίζημαι (dízēmai, “to seek”), Proto-Indo-European *yeh₂- (“to go, seek”), whence ζῆλος (zêlos, “zeal”) and ζημία (zēmía, “damage, loss”).

127.t: From Proto-Hellenic *pʰulát͏̌t͏̌ō, equal to φύλαξ (phŭ́lăx, “watcher, guard”) + *-ϳω (*-jō). Further etymology is unknown.

182.t: Unclear. Could be related to ἐλελεῦ (eleleû, “woe, alas”), which is likely expressive or onomatopoeic.

119.t: From the root of ἁμαρτάνω (hamartánō, “to miss, fail”) + -ία (-íā, abstract noun suffix).

128.t: From Proto-Indo-European *kl̥h₁-, zero-grade of *kelh₁- (“to call”). According to Beekes, the term perhaps emerged as a back-formation from the aorist ἐκάλεσα (ekálesa).

196.t: Seemingly from a Proto-Indo-European *ksewlo-, which is traditionally derived from Proto-Indo-European *kes- (“to scrape; to comb”) or from *ḱes- (“to cut”), and compared with Lithuanian šùlas (“post; pole; stave”), Russian шу́ло (šúlo, “garden-pole”)…

170.t: PIE word *swé Possibly altered from *ἕκαστις (*hékăstĭs) because of its similarity to superlative adjectives -ιστος (-ĭstos), from ἑκάς (hekắs, “far off”) + τις (tĭs, “someone”).

135.t: Likely from Proto-Indo-European *h₁eǵʰs (“out”), perhaps with suffix -ρός (-rós). If so, then Latin exter (< Proto-Indo-European *h₁eǵʰs-teros) is a particularly close cognate.

120.t: PIE word *swé From Proto-Hellenic *hwe (= *ϝ̔έ (*whé), representing the accusative case), from Proto-Indo-European *swé (reflexive pronoun).

145.t: Possibly, from the same Pre-Greek root of πάταγος (pátagos, “clatter, crash”).

184.t: From Proto-Hellenic *dunamai, from a nasal-infixed form of Proto-Indo-European *dewh₂- (“to fit together”).

197.t: Inherited from Proto-Hellenic *ártos, of unknown further origin, though likely borrowed from a substrate. Compare Basque arto (“maize”), Old Spanish artal (a type of empanada).

110.t: From Proto-Indo-European *éti. Cognates include Latin et, Sanskrit अति (ati) and Old Church Slavonic отъ (otŭ).

125.t: From οἰκοδόμος (oikodómos, “builder, architect”) + -έω (-éō, denominative verbal suffix).

198.t: From Proto-Indo-European *worǵéh₂, from the root *werǵ-; equivalent to ἔρδω (érdō) + -η (-ē). Compare Proto-Celtic *wergā.

166.t: The usual explanation is to regard the base *ὀπί- (*opĭ́-) < Proto-Hellenic *opí, *opi- < Proto-Indo-European *h₁opi, as an ablaut variant of ἐπί (epĭ́, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁epi).

155.t: Etymology tree Hebrew שָׁאַל Hebrew שָׁאוּלlbor. Ancient Greek Σαούλ Learned borrowing from Hebrew שָׁאוּל (sha'úl).

183.t: Borrowed from Biblical Hebrew פַּרְעֹה (parʿōʰ), from Egyptian pr:aA (pr-ꜥꜣ, “great house”).

102.t: From Proto-Hellenic *yótsos, from earlier *Hyótyos, from Proto-Indo-European *Hyoti, adverb from *Hyós, whence ὅς (hós).

180.t: Disputed. Dialectal variants point to Proto-Hellenic *wiskʰū́s, but since the Mycenaean Greek cognate 𐀂𐀱𐀓𐀺𐀈𐀵 (i-su-ku-wo-do-to) lacks the initial /w/, it may have arisen by analogy with *ϝίς (*wī́s, “power”) (> ἴς (ī́s)).

149.t: Adverbial neuter accusative plural of σφοδρός (sphodrós).

191.t: Disputed. Perhaps from Proto-Hellenic *erewō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rew- (“to ask, inquire”), which is probably related to Icelandic raun (“trial, test”).

117.t: Fabricated by ancient grammarians as the full form of contracted ζῶ (zô), but this is truly from ζώω (zṓō), from Proto-Hellenic *d͏̌ṓwō, from *gʷyṓwō, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷyéh₃woh₂. Doublet of βιόω (bĭóō).
